At its lowest, along the Caspian shore, it lies about 28 m below sea level.
Q737789.w: A flat, pale-brown plain with white salt lakes and sandy patches, crossed by the green ribbon of the Volga.
f: Lake Elton, in the north of the lowland, is the largest salt lake in Europe.
Lake Baskunchak has supplied Russia with salt for centuries.
Bolshoye Bogdo, only about 150 m high, is the lowland's highest point and a sacred place for the Kalmyks.

q.q: Roughly how far below sea level does the Caspian Depression reach?

Q654544.t: A green labyrinth that swallows half the White Nile
Q654544.s: Here the White Nile loses its way in the Sudd, one of the largest wetlands in the world: a vast green labyrinth of papyrus, reeds and floating plants, threaded by channels and lagoons that glint in the sun. So much water evaporates that roughly half the river's flow never leaves the swamp. Its size swells and shrinks with the rainy season.
Q654544.w: A vast, flat green swamp laced with shining channels and lagoons, with the main river winding through it.
f: Its name comes from the Arabic for 'barrier': the swamp long blocked boats travelling up the Nile.
Around AD 60 explorers sent by the Roman emperor Nero were turned back by the swamp.
The Jonglei Canal, begun in 1978 to carry water around the swamp, was never finished.

q.q: What does the Arabic name 'Sudd' mean?

Q11767.t: The land between two rivers, where writing began
Q11767.s: Mesopotamia means 'between the rivers' in Greek, and from above you can see why: the Tigris and the Euphrates run roughly side by side across a brown, dry plain, each edged with a thin green strip of fields and palms. Between them lies open steppe that turns briefly green after the winter rains. Along these rivers some of the first cities, and the first writing, appeared.
Q11767.w: A dry brown plain with two big rivers, each lined by a thin green strip of farmland, running south-east.
f: Cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems, appeared here more than 5,000 years ago.
Farming here depended on irrigation canals, some of the oldest in the world.
In southern Iraq the two rivers finally meet and flow on to the Gulf as the Shatt al-Arab.

q.q: What does the name 'Mesopotamia' mean?

Q208965.t: Where the Transantarctic Mountains meet the Ross Sea
Q208965.s: Victoria Land is Antarctica at its most dramatic: the Transantarctic Mountains rise straight from the Ross Sea, their peaks over 4,000 m, with great glaciers pouring between them onto the sea ice. Further south lie the McMurdo Dry Valleys, bare brown valleys among the driest places on Earth. James Clark Ross named this land after Queen Victoria in 1841.
Q208965.w: Jagged dark mountains and broad glaciers running down to a white, ice-covered sea; further south, bare brown valleys.
f: The McMurdo Dry Valleys are the largest ice-free area in Antarctica.
At Cape Adare, in the north, stand huts built in 1899, the first buildings on the Antarctic continent.
Italy's Mario Zucchelli Station stands on its coast, at Terra Nova Bay.

q.q: Who is Victoria Land named after?

Q1389935.t: Named after a chocolate maker who paid for the voyage
Q1389935.s: Inland from the coast, the dark peaks of the Prince Charles Mountains break through the ice of Mac. Robertson Land, while beside them the Lambert Glacier, often called the largest glacier on Earth, flows slowly north into the Amery Ice Shelf. From above, look for the long, streaked surface of moving ice between the mountains. The land honours Macpherson Robertson, an Australian chocolate maker who helped fund Mawson's 1929–31 expedition.
Q1389935.w: Dark mountain ridges poking through the ice, beside a vast, streaked glacier flowing towards a flat ice shelf.
f: Robertson's company made sweets such as the Freddo Frog chocolate.
The Lambert Glacier is more than 400 km long and up to about 100 km wide.
Australia's Mawson Station stands on its coast.

q.q: What did the man who gave Mac. Robertson Land its name make?

Q2607094.t: Where Australia set up home in Antarctica in 1954
Q2607094.s: Along the Mawson Coast the ice sheet ends in blue-white cliffs, broken by a few dark rocky headlands and islands. On one of them, in 1954, Australia built Mawson Station, the oldest station still running south of the Antarctic Circle. Behind it the Framnes Mountains poke through the ice, and fierce winds rush down the slope towards the sea.
Q2607094.w: Blue-white ice cliffs with dark rocky islands and headlands, sea ice offshore, and dark peaks poking through the ice inland.
f: The coast and the station are named after Douglas Mawson, the Australian geologist and polar explorer.
Nearby, at Auster, emperor penguins raise their chicks on the winter sea ice.
Katabatic winds pouring off the ice here often blow at gale force.

q.q: When was Mawson Station founded?

Q1576051.t: An icy coast with India's first Antarctic base
Q1576051.s: A flat ice shelf fringes the Princess Astrid Coast and meets the sea in low white cliffs. Just behind it lies the Schirmacher Oasis, a low strip of dark rock dotted with lakes that thaw in summer. Further south, where you are now, the jagged spires of the Wohlthat Mountains break through the ice, and beyond them the polar plateau begins.
Q1576051.w: A flat white ice shelf along the sea, a small dark strip of rock and lakes, then jagged mountain spires inland.
f: India's first Antarctic base, Dakshin Gangotri, was built on the ice shelf here in 1983.
By 1989 Dakshin Gangotri had been abandoned, slowly buried by snow and ice.
Russia's Novolazarevskaya and India's Maitri stations stand side by side in the Schirmacher Oasis.

q.q: Which country's first Antarctic base was built here in 1983?

Q1663286.t: Ice-free hills and salty lakes beside a giant ice shelf
Q1663286.s: Along the Ingrid Christensen Coast the ice sheet parts in places to reveal low hills of bare brown rock scattered with lakes, some of them saltier than the sea. These oases, the Vestfold and Larsemann Hills, are rare in Antarctica, and several countries have built stations among them. To the west lies the vast, flat Amery Ice Shelf.
Q1663286.w: White ice with patches of bare brown hills and small lakes along the coast; a vast, flat ice shelf to the west.
f: Deep Lake in the Vestfold Hills is so salty that it stays liquid at around −18 °C.
Australia's Davis Station stands in the Vestfold Hills; Russia, China and India have stations in the Larsemann Hills.
The coast is named after Ingrid Christensen, wife of the Norwegian whaling magnate Lars Christensen.

q.q: What makes the Vestfold Hills unusual in Antarctica?
q.a: They are largely free of ice

Q21471424.t: Where the first Soviet Antarctic station was built
Q21471424.s: The Queen Mary Coast is edged by the Shackleton Ice Shelf, a flat white platform of floating ice that ends at the sea in cliffs, with icebergs crowding below. Behind it the ice sheet rises gently inland. In 1956 the Soviet Union built Mirny here, its first Antarctic station, and Russia still runs it today.
Q21471424.w: A flat white ice shelf ending in cliffs over dark water scattered with icebergs; the ice sheet rising gently behind.
f: Mawson's Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911–14 named it after Queen Mary, wife of King George V.
Mawson's western party spent the winter of 1912 on the Shackleton Ice Shelf.
Emperor penguins breed on the sea ice near Mirny.

q.q: Which station, founded here in 1956, was the first Soviet base in Antarctica?

Q2944697.t: An oasis of lakes spotted from the air in 1947
Q2944697.s: Along the Knox Coast the ice sheet flows down to the sea in broad glaciers, but at its western end lies a surprise: the Bunger Hills, a patch of bare, low rock dotted with dozens of lakes. From the air it looks like a brown island in a white sea. US Navy pilot David Bunger spotted it in 1947, and it now bears his name.
Q2944697.w: White ice sloping down to the sea, with a striking patch of bare brown hills and lakes near the western end.
f: The coast is named after Samuel Knox, a ship's commander on the US Exploring Expedition of 1838–42.
The Bunger Hills are one of the largest ice-free areas on the Antarctic coast.
In 1956 the Soviet Union opened a station called Oazis in the Bunger Hills.

q.q: What did a pilot discover on this coast in 1947?

Q124971.t: Where a great East Antarctic glacier meets the sea
Q124971.s: On the Sabrina Coast the ice of East Antarctica pours into the ocean through the Totten Glacier, one of the largest on the continent, which ends in a floating tongue of ice. Scientists have found warm ocean water reaching beneath it, and they watch it closely. From above, look for streaked, crevassed ice meeting a sea scattered with icebergs.
Q124971.w: Crevassed, streaked ice flowing into a floating ice tongue, with icebergs and sea ice on the dark water beyond.
f: The coast takes its name from the Sabrina, a cutter of John Balleny's British expedition of 1839.
The Totten Glacier drains a basin holding enough ice to raise world sea level by several metres.
The Moscow University Ice Shelf also lies along this coast.

q.q: What is the Sabrina Coast named after?

Q21489984.t: The windy coast that gave its name to a penguin
Q21489984.s: The Adélie Coast is a short stretch of ice cliffs and rocky islets, where fierce winds pour off the ice sheet towards the sea. The French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville landed here in 1840 and named the land after his wife, Adèle. The Adélie penguin, which nests on its rocky islands, carries the same name.
Q21489984.w: Ice cliffs broken by dark rocky islets, with sea ice and icebergs offshore and the ice sheet rising steadily inland.
f: France's Dumont d'Urville Station stands on a small island just off this coast.
Its katabatic winds are among the strongest in Antarctica.
The film 'March of the Penguins' was shot among emperor penguins near Dumont d'Urville Station.

q.q: Who was the Adélie Coast named after?

Q728390.t: The icy coast where the ozone hole was found
Q728390.s: Coats Land runs down the eastern side of the Weddell Sea, where the ice sheet slides off the land into broad ice shelves. On one of them, the Brunt Ice Shelf, stands Britain's Halley station, whose measurements revealed the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985. From above there is little but white: flat shelves, long cracks and the edge of the sea ice.
Q728390.w: Flat white ice shelves with long cracks meeting the frozen Weddell Sea; the ice sheet rising gently inland.
f: Halley VI stands on legs with skis so it can be towed; in 2017 it was moved away from a growing crack.
The land was named in 1904 after James and Andrew Coats, Scottish sponsors of William Speirs Bruce's expedition.
Emperor penguins breed on the sea ice along this coast.

q.q: What did measurements at Halley station reveal in 1985?

Q1134547.s: In Ellsworth Land the Ellsworth Mountains rise from the ice like a great wall some 350 km long, and among them stands Vinson Massif, at 4,892 m the highest point in Antarctica. Around them the ice sheet stretches flat and white towards the Ronne Ice Shelf and the Bellingshausen Sea. Lincoln Ellsworth crossed this land in 1935 on the first flight across Antarctica.
Q1134547.w: A long wall of dark, jagged mountains rising from the white ice sheet, with flat ice stretching away on all sides.
f: The Sentinel Range, the northern part of the Ellsworth Mountains, holds Antarctica's highest peaks.
Climbers reach Vinson from a camp on the ice at Union Glacier, served by flights from Chile.
Vinson was first climbed only in 1966.

q.q: How high is Vinson Massif?

Q136270.t: A lonely coast first glimpsed by a sealer in 1833
Q136270.s: Kemp Land is one of the quietest corners of East Antarctica: a smooth white slope of ice running down to low ice cliffs, bays and a scatter of small rocky islands. Few people have ever set foot here. The coast was first sighted in 1833 by Peter Kemp, a British sealing captain searching the Southern Ocean for new hunting grounds.
Q136270.w: A smooth white ice slope ending in low ice cliffs and bays, with a scatter of dark rocky islets and sea ice.
f: Kemp was sailing the brig Magnet when he sighted the coast.
Mawson's BANZARE expedition charted its coastline in 1930 from the ship Discovery.
It lies between Enderby Land to the west and Mac. Robertson Land to the east.

q.q: Who was Peter Kemp, who sighted this coast in 1833?

Q4084201.t: The glacier road Shackleton took towards the Pole
Q4084201.s: Here the Transantarctic Mountains meet the western edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, and huge glaciers such as the Nimrod and the Beardmore squeeze between the peaks down onto the flat ice. In 1908–09 Ernest Shackleton's party climbed the Beardmore towards the South Pole and turned back only about 180 km short. From above, look for long rivers of ice striped with dark moraine.
Q4084201.w: Dark, snow-streaked mountains with broad glaciers flowing down onto the flat, white Ross Ice Shelf.
f: The coast was named after Sir Ernest Shackleton in 1961.
The Nimrod Glacier is named after the ship of Shackleton's 1907–09 expedition.
The Beardmore Glacier, at the coast's southern end, is about 200 km long, one of the largest valley glaciers on Earth.

q.q: About how far from the South Pole did Shackleton's party turn back?

Q2983463.t: A coast named after an expedition's initials
Q2983463.s: Along the Banzare Coast the ice sheet slides into the sea in walls of blue-white cliffs, with icebergs drifting offshore and a band of sea ice for much of the year. The name is an acronym: BANZARE, the British Australian and New Zealand Antarctic Research Expedition. Led by Douglas Mawson, it charted this coast in 1931.
Q2983463.w: Blue-white ice cliffs along the sea, icebergs and a belt of sea ice offshore, smooth white ice rising behind.
f: BANZARE sailed in the Discovery, the ship Robert Falcon Scott had taken to Antarctica in 1901.
Far inland the ice rises to Dome C, over 3,200 m high, home to the French–Italian Concordia station.
The coast lies close to the Antarctic Circle, so in midsummer the sun barely sets.

q.q: Where does the name Banzare come from?

Q2983473.t: A line of ice cliffs named after a captain's wife
Q2983473.s: The Clarie Coast is a long line of ice cliffs where the East Antarctic ice sheet meets the sea, broken here and there by glacier tongues and stranded icebergs. In January 1840 Jules Dumont d'Urville's ships sailed along these cliffs. He named the coast after Claire, wife of Charles Jacquinot, captain of his second ship, the Zélée.
Q2983473.w: A long line of white ice cliffs with jutting glacier tongues and stranded icebergs, sea ice spreading offshore.
f: An American expedition under Charles Wilkes was charting the same coast that very month.
Australia calls this stretch the Wilkes Coast.
It lies between the Banzare Coast to the west and Adélie Land to the east.

q.q: Who was Claire, after whom the Clarie Coast is named?

Q2576481.t: Rocky islands where Australia's Casey Station stands
Q2576481.s: Along the Budd Coast the ice sheet ends in cliffs and glaciers, but a scatter of low rocky islands, the Windmill Islands, breaks the white. On a rocky peninsula facing them stands Australia's Casey Station, one of its three permanent bases on the continent. Offshore, the sea freezes into a wide belt of fast ice in winter.
Q2576481.w: Low dark rocky islands and peninsulas at the edge of white ice cliffs, with sea ice spreading offshore.
f: The coast is named after Thomas Budd, an officer on Charles Wilkes's US expedition of 1838–42.
Casey Station is named after Richard Casey, an Australian politician who later became governor-general.
Adélie penguins nest on the Windmill Islands in summer.

q.q: Which country runs Casey Station on the Budd Coast?

Q21489993.t: A lone extinct volcano on an icy coast
Q21489993.s: The Wilhelm II Coast is mostly smooth ice meeting the sea, but it holds one oddity: Gaussberg, a dark, rounded extinct volcano about 370 m high, standing alone at the edge of the ice. It was found in 1902 by Erich von Drygalski's German expedition, whose ship Gauss was frozen into the sea ice nearby for almost a year. The coast is named after the German emperor Wilhelm II.
Q21489993.w: Smooth white ice meeting the sea, with a single dark, dome-shaped hill standing out near the coast.
f: The Gauss stayed locked in the ice from February 1902 to February 1903.
Drygalski's team sent up a tethered balloon to look inland, one of the first flights in Antarctica.
Gaussberg is named after the ship, which honoured the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss.

q.q: What is Gaussberg?

Q1634150.t: Japan's Antarctic home on an icy bay
Q1634150.s: The Prince Harald Coast wraps around Lützow-Holm Bay, a wide inlet usually packed with sea ice and dotted with rocky islands. On one of them, East Ongul Island, stands Japan's Syowa Station, opened in 1957. Inland the ice sheet rises steadily towards the polar plateau, broken near the coast by small patches of bare rock.
Q1634150.w: A broad bay filled with white sea ice and dotted with dark islands, the ice sheet rising behind it.
f: It is named after Prince Harald of Norway, who later became King Harald V.
Japan's icebreaker Shirase often has to ram its way through thick sea ice to reach Syowa.
Lützow-Holm Bay is named after Finn Lützow-Holm, a Norwegian naval pilot who flew over this region.

q.q: Which country runs Syowa Station on this coast?

Q1578672.t: A quiet coast named after a future king
Q1578672.s: East of Lützow-Holm Bay, the Prince Olav Coast is a stretch of low ice cliffs and glacier tongues where the ice sheet meets the sea, with sea ice clinging to the shore much of the year. Inland, the white slope climbs steadily towards the high plateau, broken only by a few dark nunataks. It is named after Crown Prince Olav of Norway.
Q1578672.w: Low ice cliffs and glacier tongues with sea ice along the shore, and a white slope rising gently inland.
f: Olav later reigned as King Olav V of Norway, from 1957 to 1991.
Norwegian expeditions of the 1930s named many coasts of Queen Maud Land after members of the royal family.
Japanese scientists from nearby Syowa Station have surveyed and mapped much of this coast.

q.q: Who was Prince Olav, after whom this coast is named?

Q928344.t: Where Antarctica was first sighted, in 1820
Q928344.s: The Princess Martha Coast is fringed by broad, flat ice shelves that end at the sea in white walls. Off this coast, in January 1820, the Russian expedition of Bellingshausen and Lazarev sighted a vast ice barrier, often counted as the first sighting of Antarctica. Today Germany's Neumayer station sits on the ice shelf, and South Africa's SANAE IV on a rocky outcrop inland.
Q928344.w: Flat white ice shelves ending in low cliffs at the sea; inland, dark rocky outcrops and mountains break the ice.
f: The coast is named after Crown Princess Märtha of Norway, wife of Crown Prince Olav.
Neumayer Station III stands on hydraulic legs, so it can be raised as the snow builds up around it.
SANAE IV, South Africa's Antarctic base, perches on a nunatak called Vesleskarvet.

q.q: Who sighted an ice shelf off this coast in January 1820?

Q6111648.t: Where the vast Thwaites Glacier meets the sea
Q6111648.s: On the Walgreen Coast the West Antarctic ice sheet reaches the Amundsen Sea through some of the fastest-changing glaciers on Earth, above all the Thwaites Glacier, about the size of Florida. From above you would see a jumble of crevassed ice breaking into icebergs, with pack ice beyond. The coast is named after Charles Walgreen of the drugstore chain, who helped fund Richard Byrd's 1933–35 expedition.
Q6111648.w: A chaos of crevassed, broken ice and icebergs where glaciers meet a sea choked with pack ice.
f: Thwaites Glacier rests on a bed far below sea level, which makes it sensitive to warm ocean water.
Scientists drill through the ice and send robots beneath it to measure how fast it is melting.
Pine Island Glacier, another fast-flowing giant, lies just to the east.

q.q: Which glacier on this coast is about the size of Florida?

Q5255259.t: The far edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, below the mountains
Q5255259.s: At the Gould Coast the flat Ross Ice Shelf, the largest ice shelf on Earth, meets the foot of the Transantarctic Mountains, where glaciers such as the Scott Glacier pour down between dark peaks. This is one of the most remote places on the planet, only about 650 km from the South Pole. It is named after Laurence Gould, the geologist who led a dog-sledge party here in 1929.
Q5255259.w: The flat white ice shelf meeting a wall of dark, snowy mountains, with broad glaciers flowing out between them.
f: Gould was second-in-command of Richard Byrd's 1928–30 expedition; his party mapped some 280 km of this coast.
The Scott Glacier, discovered by Gould's party in 1929, is named after Robert Falcon Scott, who never saw it.
The Ross Ice Shelf is roughly the size of France and hundreds of metres thick.

q.q: Who was Laurence Gould, after whom this coast is named?

Q1551170.t: The high, icy base of the Antarctic Peninsula
Q1551170.s: Palmer Land is the broad southern part of the Antarctic Peninsula, where the narrow mountain spine widens into a high, ice-covered plateau cut by glaciers flowing to both coasts. To the west, look for George VI Sound, a long, straight channel filled with an ice shelf, separating it from Alexander Island. It is named after Nathaniel Palmer, an American sealer who sailed these waters in 1820.
Q1551170.w: A high white plateau with glaciers running off both sides; to the west, a long, straight ice-filled channel.
f: The US Palmer Station is not in Palmer Land at all, but far north on Anvers Island, off Graham Land.
Its mountains rise to more than 3,000 m.
Nathaniel Palmer was only 21 when he sailed his sloop Hero into these waters.

q.q: Where is the US Palmer Station?

Q618370.s: Graham Land is the northern arm of the Antarctic Peninsula, a narrow, rugged spine of mountains draped in glaciers that reaches up towards South America. Its west coast is a maze of channels, islands and ice cliffs visited by most tourist ships to Antarctica. On its east coast lie the Larsen ice shelves, parts of which broke apart in 1995 and 2002.
Q618370.w: A narrow spine of jagged, glacier-draped mountains between two icy seas, with ice shelves along the eastern side.
f: John Biscoe named it in 1832 after Sir James Graham, First Lord of the Admiralty.
The tip of the peninsula lies only about 1,000 km from South America, across the Drake Passage.
The Lemaire Channel on its west coast is so narrow and dramatic that it is nicknamed 'Kodak Gap'.

q.q: Which passage separates Graham Land from South America?

Q1145030.t: The very tip of the Horn of Africa
Q1145030.s: Here Africa comes to a point. At Cape Guardafui the coast of the Horn, running east along the Gulf of Aden, turns sharply south into the Indian Ocean. From above, look for a bare, tan headland with pale cliffs and beaches, where turquoise shallows meet the deep blue sea. Ships bound to and from the Red Sea pass it every day.
Q1145030.w: A bare, tan headland where the coast turns sharply from east to south, pale cliffs above turquoise and deep blue sea.
f: Ancient Greek sailors knew it as Aromata, the 'Cape of Spices'.
Africa's easternmost point is not here but at Ras Hafun, about 150 km to the south.
The cape marks the boundary between the Gulf of Aden and the open Indian Ocean.

q.q: Which body of water lies north of Cape Guardafui?

Q193401.t: A hook of sand where rockets leave the Earth
Q193401.s: Look for a hook of sand jutting from Florida's Atlantic coast, with lagoons and marshes behind it: Cape Canaveral. Rockets have launched from here since the 1950s, and the Apollo missions to the Moon left from the Kennedy Space Center next door, on Merritt Island. With luck you might even see a launch plume climbing from the coast.
Q193401.w: A pointed hook of sand on Florida's Atlantic coast, backed by broad lagoons and marshes.
f: From 1963 to 1973 the cape was officially called Cape Kennedy.
Its name comes from the Spanish 'cañaveral', a place where cane grows.
Rockets launch eastwards over the Atlantic, so spent stages fall into the sea rather than on land.

q.q: Which Moon missions launched from beside Cape Canaveral?

Q780339.t: California's westernmost point, where three plates meet
Q780339.s: At Cape Mendocino the rugged Lost Coast of northern California juts furthest into the Pacific, its steep green hills dropping straight into the surf. Just offshore, three plates of the Earth's crust meet at the Mendocino Triple Junction, making this one of the most earthquake-prone corners of the United States. Look for a dark headland with a long white line of breakers.
Q780339.w: A dark, steep headland where the northern California coast bulges furthest west, fringed with white surf.
f: Cape Mendocino is the westernmost point of California.
The Lost Coast around it is so steep that the coastal highway turns inland to avoid it.
Spanish galleons sailing from Manila to Mexico often used the cape as their first landmark in America.

q.q: How many tectonic plates meet off Cape Mendocino?

Q1020776.t: The rocky tip of Baja California, where two seas meet
Q1020776.s: At the very end of the long, dry Baja California peninsula, granite cliffs break into the sea at Land's End, where the Gulf of California meets the open Pacific. From above, look for the sharp southern tip of the peninsula, a curved bay with white beaches and the resort town around it. In winter humpback whales gather in these warm waters.
Q1020776.w: The sharp southern tip of a long desert peninsula: pale granite cliffs, a curved bay and a town along its shore.
f: El Arco, a natural stone arch at Land's End, is the town's best-known landmark.
The Baja California peninsula stretches some 1,200 km from the US border to this cape.
The Tropic of Cancer passes just north of the town.

q.q: Which waters meet at Cabo San Lucas?

ne-rg-1159105013.t: Where polar bears wait for the sea to freeze
ne-rg-1159105013.s: On the flat western shore of Hudson Bay, Cape Churchill pushes into the sea, a low point of tundra, lakes and gravel beaches. Every autumn polar bears gather here and near the town of Churchill, waiting for the bay to freeze so they can hunt seals on the ice. Much of the land around lies in Wapusk National Park, one of the largest polar bear denning areas in the world.
ne-rg-1159105013.w: A low, flat point of tundra dotted with countless lakes, jutting into Hudson Bay; white with ice much of the year.
f: The nearby town of Churchill calls itself the 'Polar Bear Capital of the World'.
Each summer thousands of beluga whales gather in the Churchill River estuary.
The treeline runs close by, so forest, tundra and sea ice all meet in this corner of Manitoba.

q.q: Why do polar bears gather near Cape Churchill in autumn?
q.a: To wait for the sea ice
